content: 1. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials, as well as observational studies (including case-control, cohort, and crossover studies), were included in the analysis. Only fully peer-reviewed articles with complete text available in English were considered, with no restrictions on publication date. 2. The outcomes assessed included gait, cognition, and dual-tasking abilities. A meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of circuit-based exercises on gait speed, balance, and functional mobility in individuals affected by stroke. 3. Circuit-based exercises were found to improve gait speed more effectively than conventional interventions. However, their effects on balance and functional mobility were not significantly better than those of conventional interventions. 4. Aerobic exercise (AEX) was shown to significantly improve aerobic capacity (measured by peak oxygen consumption, VO2 peak) in post-stroke patients. Higher AEX intensity and better baseline VO2 peak were associated with larger improvements in aerobic capacity. Walking-based AEX was more effective in improving walking speed and endurance compared to seated AEX. 5. Nordic walking (NW) was identified as a promising activity for individuals with cardiovascular disease (CVD). It demonstrated additional health benefits when combined with conventional cardiovascular rehabilitation (CCVR) programs. However, no significant differences were observed between NW and CCVR in heart failure patients for peak VO2 and functional mobility. 6. Traditional Chinese exercises (TCEs) were found to have positive effects on limb motor function, balance, activities of daily living (ADL), and neurological impairment in stroke patients. These benefits were consistent across different types of TCEs and intervention durations. However, TCEs did not improve physical function as measured by the Short Physical Performance Battery and 2-minute Step Test. 7. Resistance training protocols for improving mobility outcomes after stroke varied widely in their adherence to the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) guidelines. While training frequency was consistently high, adherence to intensity, specificity, and training patterns was low. Future trials should ensure closer adherence to ACSM guidelines to accurately determine the effectiveness of resistance training. 8. Walking training interventions, including overground and treadmill walking, were effective in improving walking speed, distance, and gait speed in stroke survivors. Some interventions augmented by auditory stimulation showed significant improvements in physical function compared to overground walking alone. However, not all interventions maintained locomotor improvements at follow-up. 9. Tai Chi was found to have short-term benefits for improving balance and gait in stroke survivors. However, the included studies had high bias and small sample sizes. Larger, long-term randomized controlled trials with standardized evaluation methods are needed to confirm these findings. 10. Pilates was identified as an effective intervention for promoting healthy behaviors and physical activity in individuals with chronic diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes. However, the evidence for its effects in non-communicable diseases (NCDs) has not been fully systematized, and further research is needed.
